findings: The scene is an indoor room lit by ceiling strip lights. The flicker of those lights carries a strong grid signal (73% of the clip usable). The audio mains hum is too weak to use, so it was not relied on.
Around the stated time on 10 Nov 2026 nothing matched well: the best score was 0.78, and several unrelated times scored almost the same. That is what chance looks like.
Searching 5 to 15 November gave one clear match: 8 Nov 2026 at 11:44:08 UTC, scoring 0.971. The best match on any other day scored 0.877.
Check 1 (sharpness): moving the start 10 s either way drops the score to about 0.89, and 60 s either way drops it to about 0.57. The fit points to one moment, not a broad stretch of time.
Check 2 (two halves): the first and second halves of the clip, matched separately, each give a start within 3 s of 11:44:08 on 8 Nov. There is no sign the clip was spliced from different times.
Check 3 (other days): the same time of day on the neighbouring days matches clearly worse (0.83 to 0.88).
The grid record used for this period samples every 15 seconds. That is enough to fix the date and the minute firmly, but not to name the exact second.
input.what_it_means: The time of day on the recording is right, but the date looks wrong by two days. The video appears to have been made on Sunday 8 November, not Tuesday 10 November. This pattern fits a mistaken date (wrong date setting, mislabelling, or confusion between files). It also fits footage from another day being offered as if it were from the 10th. The timing evidence cannot say which. If the case depends on events on 10 November, this recording does not show them.
